title: How the canon took shape
scope: Selected evidence for formation and reception, not an exhaustive canon history or a judgment between traditions.
authorization: The current user explicitly requested research, design and implementation of study 04, superseding the programme’s earlier first-pass-only sequence for this study.
teachingSequence: Distinguish quotation, public reading, copying, recommendation and explicit canonical recognition.
Locate each text, codex and decision within its date, place and genre.
Test competing explanations of 11Q5, then separate rabbinic evidence from a modern closure narrative.
Compare the categories used by Athanasius, Augustine and Jerome; preserve Eusebius’s conditional judgments.
Inspect Alexandrinus’s surviving and missing contents; distinguish the Peshitta version from modern church boundaries.
Follow individual writings and compare named traditions without a privileged baseline.
Practice warranted inference and pursue the explicitly graded scholarly reading trail.

evidenceKinds.meaning: A writer uses words from a work. The authority of this passage does not specify the boundaries of a whole collection.

evidenceKinds.example: Justin describes readings in Sunday worship.
evidenceKinds.meaning: A community hears a writing in worship. Ask which community, which setting and what authority the source assigns it.

evidenceKinds.example: Sinaiticus transmits Barnabas and Hermas beside New Testament books.
evidenceKinds.meaning: A physical object contains a work. A codex is evidence of transmission; inclusion alone is not an explicit declaration of canonical status.
A writing can be valued for teaching while being excluded from the same author’s canonical list.
An authority identifies a bounded collection as Scripture. Ask whose authority, at what date and with what reach.

records.title: An inherited body of writings
records.evidence: The translator of Sirach names the Law, the Prophets and other ancestral books. He describes his arrival in Egypt in the king’s thirty-eighth year, conventionally 132 BCE.
records.interpretation: Recognizable collections predate this translation. The unnamed third group need not have had exactly the boundaries of the later Writings.
records.limit: The arrival date is not the date of completion. This prologue supplies no complete book list.

records.title: A collection is not a table of contents
records.evidence: The caves preserve biblical writings alongside other religious works, including Jubilees. The IAA reports no identified copy of Esther among the Qumran biblical scrolls.
records.interpretation: The finds reveal circulation and preservation. Their modern classification as biblical or non-biblical uses later collections as a reference.
records.limit: Absence among surviving finds does not establish rejection. Nor is every copied work necessarily scripture for every community.

records.title: A quotation has a particular reach
records.evidence: Jude 14–15 presents an Enochic prophecy; the USCCB note identifies the passage with 1 Enoch 1:9.
records.interpretation: The writer treats this saying as useful and authoritative in the argument.
records.limit: Quoting this passage does not, by itself, identify a complete collection of Enochic writings or establish its reception in every church.

records.place: Rome · Justin’s account of Christian worship
records.title: What the congregation hears
records.evidence: Justin describes Sunday readings from apostolic memoirs or prophetic writings, followed by the leader’s instruction. He calls the memoirs Gospels in the preceding chapter.
records.interpretation: Public worship helped transmit and authorize particular writings through repeated use.
records.limit: This description is not an exhaustive named list of New Testament books. It cannot tell us everything read in every church.

records.place: Lyons · Greek Christian argument, preserved in translation
records.title: Why four Gospels? An argument, not a council vote.
records.evidence: Against Heresies 3.11.7–9 defends Matthew, Mark, Luke and John together. Irenaeus appeals to the four winds and four living creatures, and criticizes opponents for using fewer or more gospels.
records.interpretation: The passage witnesses a vigorously defended fourfold Gospel. Its cosmic symbolism is a theological rationale for the collection he receives, not independent historical proof that four books had to be chosen.
records.limit: A polemical author’s account of opponents is not their own testimony. This passage neither enumerates the whole New Testament nor records the moment the fourfold collection began.
contents: Read 3.11.7 for his presentation of rival use.
Distinguish his defended norm from a census of all Christian readers.

records.place: Often placed at Rome · origin disputed
records.title: Read it — but not in that setting
records.evidence: The damaged list names Luke as the third Gospel and John as the fourth. It allows reading Hermas but excludes it from public reading among prophets or apostles. Reception of the Apocalypse of Peter is qualified.
records.interpretation: The writer draws boundaries using apostolic-era origins and suitability for church reading. Missing opening material must be reconstructed, not silently supplied.
records.limit: The medieval Latin copy is later than the proposed composition. Hahneman argues for a fourth-century eastern list; Guignard distinguishes a later Latin text from an earlier composition. These research abstracts, not the full works, were consulted.
contents: John’s Apocalypse; Peter’s Apocalypse with qualification
Hermas — recommended, public scriptural reading excluded

records.title: A debate about sacred scrolls
records.evidence: Yadayim 3:5 preserves differing opinions about Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes within rules about scrolls making hands ritually impure. Akiva strongly defends Song of Songs.
records.interpretation: The ritual category marks sacred status in this discussion; its vocabulary should not be flattened into a modern ballot on a Bible.
records.limit: A transmitted debate about these scrolls is not a surviving record of one council choosing the entire Jewish canon at Yavneh (Jamnia).

records.title: Agreement, disagreement, rejection
records.evidence: Eusebius distinguishes accepted writings from disputed ones, including James, Jude, 2 Peter and 2–3 John. Revelation appears conditionally in both accepted and rejected groupings. Elsewhere he reports public reading of Hermas.
records.interpretation: His classifications describe a field of reception and also express judgments about authenticity.
records.limit: The labels are his categories, not a census of all Christians. “Disputed” is not a single uniform degree of authority.
contents: Accepted: four Gospels, Acts, Pauline letters, 1 John, 1 Peter

books.Hermas: Outside acknowledged books; public use reported

records.title: Bound together on the page
records.evidence: Sinaiticus preserves the complete New Testament alongside Barnabas and surviving portions of Hermas; its Old Testament is now incomplete.
records.interpretation: The codex shows these works being transmitted together. Its physical contents need not map exactly onto a later list’s categories.
records.limit: Neither the place of copying nor a commission by Constantine is established here. Do not convert material inclusion into a universal ecclesiastical decree.

records.title: Two lists, two purposes
records.evidence: Athanasius enumerates the familiar 27 New Testament books. His Old Testament includes Baruch with Jeremiah. He places Esther and Hermas among books for instruction outside his canon.
records.interpretation: His distinction lets us observe recommendation without equating it with canonical recognition.
records.limit: This is a bishop’s prescription to his readers, not evidence of simultaneous agreement everywhere.
contents: Jeremiah includes Baruch, Lamentations and the Letter
For instruction: Wisdom, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, Didache, Hermas

records.title: Reception becomes a criterion
records.evidence: Augustine advises weighing the reception of books among churches. His enumeration includes Tobit, Judith, two Maccabees, Wisdom and Sirach, as well as Esther and the 27 New Testament books.
records.interpretation: A different Old Testament scope coexists with the same New Testament enumeration seen in Athanasius.
records.limit: His account of authority is an argument within a church tradition, not a neutral survey. Ancient counts and book divisions differ.

records.place: Latin translation programme · addressed to Chromatius and Heliodorus
records.title: Books may instruct without establishing doctrine.
records.evidence: In his prologue to Solomon’s books, Jerome separates Wisdom and Sirach from canonical Scripture while allowing edifying reading. He compares their use with Judith, Tobit and Maccabees.
records.interpretation: His concern is what can establish church doctrine. A translated or read work need not have that status in his account. Compare Augustine’s recognition of Wisdom and Sirach in the same broad period.
records.limit: This prologue states a position; it is not a survey of all Latin churches or a complete account of every use Jerome makes of these books.
contents: The three translated books here are Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs.
Wisdom and Sirach are discussed separately.
His distinction concerns authority and use, not simply physical availability.

records.place: Syriac-speaking Christianity · version and manuscript tradition
records.title: A New Testament collection of twenty-two books.
records.evidence: The Peshitta New Testament has twenty-two books, without 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude and Revelation. The Gorgias reference entry dates its emergence as the standard version to around 400.
records.interpretation: A Greek or Latin list does not describe every contemporary Christian collection. Translation and transmission have their own histories.
records.limit: This describes the Peshitta version, not every later Syriac Bible or the present canon of every Syriac church. A version’s emergence and the date of an extant copy are separate questions.
contents: Add. 14470 is assigned to the fifth/sixth century in the manuscript survey.
The five writings absent from the Peshitta should not be treated as missing leaves in these descriptions.

books.Revelation: Not part of the twenty-two-book Peshitta version.

records.title: A rule for reading as Scripture
records.evidence: Canon 24 of the African Code limits reading under the name of divine Scripture to an enumerated collection, including Tobit, Judith and two Maccabees. Its New Testament corresponds to 27 books.
records.interpretation: A church decision regulates received practice and seeks wider confirmation; it does not create the texts or their first use.
records.limit: The 419 compilation transmits earlier decisions, associated with Hippo (393) and Carthage (397). Those dates should not be treated as three independent surviving transcripts. Its jurisdiction is not the whole Christian world.
contents: Canonical list for public scriptural reading
Request for confirmation from Boniface and other bishops

records.place: Eastern Mediterranean · now British Library, Royal MS 1 D VIII
records.title: A codex ends beyond Revelation—and then breaks off.
records.evidence: After Revelation, Alexandrinus preserves 1 Clement and part of 2 Clement. A contents list in volume 1 also names Psalms of Solomon, separated by a space; that work is not preserved in the codex.
records.interpretation: The surviving leaves and the contents list offer different evidence. The catalogue infers loss; the named work cannot be inspected here as surviving text.
records.limit: The arrangement establishes a collection, not equal canonical rank for every component. The damaged ending prevents a complete description from surviving leaves alone.
contents: 1 Clement: ff. 134r–143r, with a missing leaf.
Psalms of Solomon: contents-list notice at Royal MS 1 D V, f. 4r; no surviving text here.

books.Revelation: Copied before 1 Clement and the surviving portion of 2 Clement.

records.title: A collection also has an order
records.evidence: Bava Batra 14b transmits an order of the Prophets and Writings. The latter begins with Ruth, Psalms and Job, and ends with Ezra and Chronicles.
records.interpretation: Naming and ordering books is another way a collection is made visible. Order need not match that of a later printed Tanakh.
records.limit: The date of a compilation is not automatically the date of every tradition it preserves. This study does not date this list to a single year.

records.title: A confessionally binding enumeration
records.evidence: Trent’s fourth session receives a named set of Old and New Testament books with their parts, including Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and two Maccabees.
records.interpretation: The decree gives a binding Catholic definition amid Reformation controversy. Earlier lists already attest much of this collection.
records.limit: This decision does not describe the canon of every Jewish or Christian tradition. The decree’s Vulgate wording also concerns the received parts of books.
contents: Named Old and New Testament books
Books received with all their parts
Scripture and apostolic tradition addressed together

records.title: A different boundary is confessed
records.evidence: Chapter 1 enumerates 39 Old Testament and 27 New Testament books, then excludes the writings it calls Apocrypha from the canon.
records.interpretation: A shared New Testament collection does not erase disagreement about other writings or about how their authority is established.
records.limit: The linked OPC edition is a received denominational form, not a facsimile of the original assembly manuscript. It represents Reformed reception, not every Protestant practice.

traditions.name: Jewish · Tanakh
traditions.scope: Torah, Prophets and Writings; conventionally 24 books. This is a collection in its own right, not an incomplete Christian Bible.
traditions.note: Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra–Nehemiah and the Twelve are grouped differently from many Christian editions. Equivalent book counts do not establish identical textual forms.

traditions.name: Roman Catholic
traditions.scope: 46 Old Testament books and 27 New Testament books in the Catechism’s enumeration.
traditions.note: “Deuterocanonical” names books with a distinct reception history; it does not make them a lower grade of Catholic Scripture.

traditions.name: Reformed · Westminster
traditions.scope: 39 Old Testament books and 27 New Testament books; the confession excludes Apocrypha from the canon.
traditions.note: Printing other writings beside Scripture would not reverse this stated boundary. This entry does not stand for every Protestant church.

traditions.name: Anglican · Article VI
traditions.context: Church of England · Articles of Religion
traditions.scope: Article VI separates canonical books from other books used for moral instruction rather than to establish doctrine.
traditions.note: Its instructional list includes Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, Maccabees and the Prayer of Manasseh. Read-publicly and canonical remain distinct.
states: Canonical book; Greek portions for instruction
Canonical book; Greek portions for instruction

traditions.name: Eastern Orthodox · OCA
traditions.context: Orthodox Church in America · canon answer and Revelation exposition
traditions.scope: The OCA describes a longer Old Testament canon, including Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, Maccabees and the Prayer of Manasseh.
traditions.note: This is one Orthodox institutional explanation, not an inventory of every Greek or Slavonic edition. Its general reference to Maccabees is not used here to infer a universal book count. Its Revelation exposition explicitly separates canonical inclusion from liturgical reading.
states: Canonical; not read liturgically in this account

traditions.name: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo
traditions.context: Church’s English list · Cowley’s 1974 study of editions
traditions.scope: The source counts 81 books as 46 Old Testament and 35 New Testament; it names Enoch, Jubilees and additional church-order writings.
traditions.note: Book groupings and titles need careful translation. This source’s count is not a promise that every printed Ethiopic Bible contains all 81 in one volume. Cowley distinguishes Ethiopic Meqabyan from the Greek Maccabees books; similar English titles do not identify the same works.
states: Listed; Greek additions in editions studied by Cowley
Listed; Greek additions in editions studied by Cowley
With Jeremiah in editions studied by Cowley
Within 2 Chronicles in editions studied by Cowley

method.evidence: Record.evidence summarizes attested wording or institutional object description.
method.interpretation: Record.interpretation is this study’s inference, not a quotation or a new historical datum.
method.uncertainty: Record.limit, date and place preserve uncertainty and document scope. A questioned date is never plotted as a precise event.
method.visuals: Original typographic and CSS schematics only. Chronological register has equal spacing, not a quantitative time axis. No external manuscript images or transcriptions reproduced.
method.comparison: Selected writings, not full inventories. “Not specified” is an evidence limit, not exclusion. Two sources chosen independently; neither is the universal baseline.
method.access: Translations and institutional records were read only as specified in each source access field. Research abstracts do not imply full-work reading.

disagreements.finding: Separate surviving-copy date, Latin translation date and proposed original composition. A fixed second-century pin would overstate precision.
The selected sources attest sacred writings and debate; they do not provide a council decree fixing the entire collection.
Different dated authorities state boundaries with different scope. The sources do not warrant a single universal selection event.
Physical association, acknowledged status and instructional use must remain separate predicates.

researchLimits: This is not an exhaustive history of Samaritan, Syriac, Armenian, Georgian, Coptic or Eritrean reception. No universal Jewish or Orthodox table is inferred from the selected institutional examples.
A full critical study would collate original-language witnesses of the lists, inspect manuscript folios and consult full modern research, beyond the translations and records used here.
The Bava Batra entry uses a retrieved passage, not a full review of the folio or its redaction history.
The OCA answer’s historical generalizations are not adopted as evidence for earliest Christian agreement. Its self-description is used as reception evidence.
The general-study editorial restriction is preserved; prohibited author-specific material is not used.

investigations.purpose: Move from the type of witness to the exact claim it warrants, then compare authority, collection and survival without treating any modern canon as the default.

jewish.title: A collection before a contents page

observations.label: A reader’s vocabulary
observations.date: Sirach’s Greek prologue · grandson arrives in Egypt in 132 BCE
observations.text: The translator distinguishes law, prophets and other ancestral books. He does not name the members of the third group. A threefold description is evidence of differentiation, not a recoverable final inventory.

observations.label: An actual collected object
observations.date: 11Q5 · copy dated c. 30–50 CE by the Library of Congress
observations.text: This scroll combines familiar psalms in a different sequence with other hymns and prose about David. Found in Cave 11 in 1956 and unrolled in 1961, it makes the shape of a psalm collection visible where a later printed contents page cannot.

hypotheses.name: An alternative Psalter
hypotheses.claim: The collection witnesses a form of the Psalter before its contents and order became uniform.
hypotheses.requires: Evidence that the arrangement functioned as an authoritative collection, rather than merely preserving selected songs.
hypotheses.result: Variation becomes evidence about the developing collection itself.

hypotheses.name: An anthology for use
hypotheses.claim: The compiler selected and arranged material for a particular purpose from already valued traditions.
hypotheses.requires: Independent evidence of the earlier collection and of this scroll’s use; a difference from the later order alone cannot establish derivation.
hypotheses.result: Variation describes a new compilation; it need not redefine every source work’s boundary.

jewish.debate: Sanders’s edition (DJD IV, 1965) established the scroll’s publication. Lim traces the alternative-Psalter interpretation and objections by Goshen-Gottstein, Talmon and Skehan. The dispute concerns the collection’s authority, not merely its arrangement.
jewish.correction: Mroczek’s 2016 programme questions projecting our bounded Bible onto ancient sacred writing. Lim objects that textual fluidity and canonical authority must be distinguished. Different arrangements do not by themselves establish an absence of authoritative writings.
jewish.rabbinic: Mishnah Yadayim 3:5 debates whether Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes impart ritual impurity to hands. Akiva strongly defends the Song; the passage preserves differing voices. This is legal discussion about sacred writings, not an enumerated decree selecting an entire Bible.
jewish.yavneh: Lim traces the “Council of Jamnia” narrative to modern scholarship and its critics. This source supplies neither a complete inventory nor a closure date.
jewish.limits: The DJD edition and the earlier rebuttals were located through the institutional description and Lim’s bibliography, not independently read. No exact count of 11Q5’s biblical psalms is used: institutional and scholarly descriptions count the material differently.

witnesses.name: Athanasius
witnesses.principle: Draws a boundary around the canon, then names reading for newcomers separately.

states.label: Instruction outside the canon
states.text: Both belong to his reading list for instruction.

states.label: Instruction outside the canon
states.text: Esther appears in the instructional list, not his Old Testament enumeration.

states.label: Instruction outside the canon
states.text: The Shepherd is recommended in the same instructional category.

witnesses.excerpt: not indeed included in the Canon

witnesses.name: Augustine
witnesses.date: Latin North Africa · late 4th / early 5th century
witnesses.principle: Weighs reception among churches, including their number and apostolic standing.

states.label: Canonical
states.text: Both occur within his enumeration of authoritative books.

states.label: Not enumerated
states.text: The Shepherd is absent from this list. This is not a statement about every possible use of it.

witnesses.excerpt: follow the judgment of the greater number of Catholic churches

witnesses.name: Jerome
witnesses.passage: Prologue to the books of Solomon
witnesses.principle: Distinguishes edifying reading from authority to confirm church doctrine.

states.label: Edifying; not canonical here
states.text: Read for strengthening the people, but not to establish doctrine.

states.label: Not addressed here
states.text: This prologue does not discuss Esther. Silence in a selected passage cannot establish exclusion.

states.label: Not addressed here
states.text: This prologue does not discuss Hermas. Consult a different passage before assigning a status.

witnesses.excerpt: not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical dogmas

boundaries.insight: Athanasius and Augustine enumerate the same twenty-seven New Testament books, yet their Old Testament boundaries differ. Agreement in one collection does not establish agreement in another. “Apocrypha” also changes meaning across authors and later traditions; it is not a timeless shelf label.

eusebius.intro: Eusebius’s Church History 3.25 reports reception as well as judging it. His categories resist a single yes/no column.

clauses.label: 3.25.2 · accepted
clauses.text: Revelation is placed conditionally among accepted writings.

clauses.label: 3.25.4 · rejected
clauses.text: Revelation reappears conditionally, because some reject it and others accept it.
clauses.excerpt: which some, as I said, reject

eusebius.explanation: Both clauses belong to the same account. James, Jude, 2 Peter and 2–3 John are disputed yet known widely; Hermas belongs to another group. The works he denounces as heretical are distinguished again. These are Eusebius’s judgments and reported divisions, not neutral labels or a vote count.

codex.title: The end of a codex is not the edge of a canon
codex.shelfmark: Royal MS 1 D VIII · Codex Alexandrinus · 5th century

segments.name: Revelation
segments.note: Its text precedes the Clementine writings. Physical sequence alone does not define the canonical status of the next work.

segments.name: 1 Clement
segments.note: A leaf is missing between folios 142 and 143. The catalogue identifies the lost passage as 1 Clement 57:7–63:4. A surviving work need not survive intact.

segments.name: 2 Clement
segments.note: The surviving text stops at 12:5. This is physical incompleteness, not evidence that the compiler intended the work to stop there.

segments.name: Psalms of Solomon
segments.note: The title appears after a space in the contents list. The catalogue infers loss, but there is no surviving text of this work here. The gap in the list must not be erased in a reconstructed inventory.

codex.limits: Schematic sequence, not a facsimile, page count or reconstruction of lost leaves. Labels follow the British Library catalogue. Its digitised images were unavailable at consultation.

scholarshipGuide.question: How do we read ancient lists accurately?
scholarshipGuide.work: Edmon L. Gallagher & John D. Meade, The Biblical Canon Lists from Early Christianity (2017)
scholarshipGuide.contribution: Original-language lists with translations and interpretive notes provide a route from a modern claim back to a particular witness. Use this for detailed textual work beyond the older translations linked here.
scholarshipGuide.access: Publisher abstract and contents consulted; full book is further reading.

scholarshipGuide.question: What did sacred writing look like before “the Bible”?
scholarshipGuide.work: Eva Mroczek, The Literary Imagination in Jewish Antiquity (2016)
scholarshipGuide.contribution: Reframes the question around ancient literary imagination: growing traditions, attributed authors and writings beyond later canonical boundaries. Its programme challenges treating every ancient collection as a preliminary modern Bible.
scholarshipGuide.access: Publisher abstract consulted; full book not read.

scholarshipGuide.question: Does variation mean that there was no canon?
scholarshipGuide.work: Timothy H. Lim, The Writings in the Hellenistic-Roman Period (2018)
scholarshipGuide.contribution: Separates changing textual forms from authority, while revisiting the Psalms-scroll debate and the limits of reconstructing closure from rabbinic evidence.
scholarshipGuide.access: Relevant sections of the open peer-reviewed manuscript read; earlier studies discussed there not independently verified.

scholarshipGuide.question: How early is the Muratorian evidence?
scholarshipGuide.contribution: Dating changes how early this witness can be used. Hahneman argues for a fourth-century eastern setting. Guignard supports a Greek original, distinguishing a later fourth-century Latin text from a likely late second-century composition. A surviving copy’s date does not itself date the original.
scholarshipGuide.access: Abstracts only. The full argument and textual apparatus remain a research gap.

scholarshipGuide.question: What does an Ethiopian count of eighty-one mean?
scholarshipGuide.work: R. W. Cowley, The Biblical Canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church Today (1974)
scholarshipGuide.contribution: Relates narrower and broader lists to counting and book identities. Meqabyan must not be equated with the Greek books called Maccabees. A number without names and grouping rules is not an inventory.
scholarshipGuide.access: Relevant paragraphs of the online journal reprint read, not the printed original; not a contemporary survey of every Ethiopian edition.

claimLedger.evidence: The translator of Sirach names the Law, the Prophets and other ancestral books. He describes his arrival in Egypt in the king’s thirty-eighth year, conventionally 132 BCE.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: Recognizable collections predate this translation. The unnamed third group need not have had exactly the boundaries of the later Writings.
claimLedger.limit: The arrival date is not the date of completion. This prologue supplies no complete book list.

claimLedger.evidence: The caves preserve biblical writings alongside other religious works, including Jubilees. The IAA reports no identified copy of Esther among the Qumran biblical scrolls.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: The finds reveal circulation and preservation. Their modern classification as biblical or non-biblical uses later collections as a reference.
claimLedger.limit: Absence among surviving finds does not establish rejection. Nor is every copied work necessarily scripture for every community.

claimLedger.evidence: Jude 14–15 presents an Enochic prophecy; the USCCB note identifies the passage with 1 Enoch 1:9.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: The writer treats this saying as useful and authoritative in the argument.
claimLedger.limit: Quoting this passage does not, by itself, identify a complete collection of Enochic writings or establish its reception in every church.

claimLedger.evidence: Justin describes Sunday readings from apostolic memoirs or prophetic writings, followed by the leader’s instruction. He calls the memoirs Gospels in the preceding chapter.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: Public worship helped transmit and authorize particular writings through repeated use.
claimLedger.limit: This description is not an exhaustive named list of New Testament books. It cannot tell us everything read in every church.

claimLedger.evidence: Against Heresies 3.11.7–9 defends Matthew, Mark, Luke and John together. Irenaeus appeals to the four winds and four living creatures, and criticizes opponents for using fewer or more gospels.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: The passage witnesses a vigorously defended fourfold Gospel. Its cosmic symbolism is a theological rationale for the collection he receives, not independent historical proof that four books had to be chosen.
claimLedger.limit: A polemical author’s account of opponents is not their own testimony. This passage neither enumerates the whole New Testament nor records the moment the fourfold collection began.

claimLedger.evidence: The damaged list names Luke as the third Gospel and John as the fourth. It allows reading Hermas but excludes it from public reading among prophets or apostles. Reception of the Apocalypse of Peter is qualified.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: The writer draws boundaries using apostolic-era origins and suitability for church reading. Missing opening material must be reconstructed, not silently supplied.
claimLedger.limit: The medieval Latin copy is later than the proposed composition. Hahneman argues for a fourth-century eastern list; Guignard distinguishes a later Latin text from an earlier composition. These research abstracts, not the full works, were consulted.

claimLedger.evidence: Yadayim 3:5 preserves differing opinions about Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes within rules about scrolls making hands ritually impure. Akiva strongly defends Song of Songs.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: The ritual category marks sacred status in this discussion; its vocabulary should not be flattened into a modern ballot on a Bible.
claimLedger.limit: A transmitted debate about these scrolls is not a surviving record of one council choosing the entire Jewish canon at Yavneh (Jamnia).

claimLedger.evidence: Eusebius distinguishes accepted writings from disputed ones, including James, Jude, 2 Peter and 2–3 John. Revelation appears conditionally in both accepted and rejected groupings. Elsewhere he reports public reading of Hermas.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: His classifications describe a field of reception and also express judgments about authenticity.
claimLedger.limit: The labels are his categories, not a census of all Christians. “Disputed” is not a single uniform degree of authority.

claimLedger.evidence: Sinaiticus preserves the complete New Testament alongside Barnabas and surviving portions of Hermas; its Old Testament is now incomplete.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: The codex shows these works being transmitted together. Its physical contents need not map exactly onto a later list’s categories.
claimLedger.limit: Neither the place of copying nor a commission by Constantine is established here. Do not convert material inclusion into a universal ecclesiastical decree.

claimLedger.evidence: Athanasius enumerates the familiar 27 New Testament books. His Old Testament includes Baruch with Jeremiah. He places Esther and Hermas among books for instruction outside his canon.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: His distinction lets us observe recommendation without equating it with canonical recognition.
claimLedger.limit: This is a bishop’s prescription to his readers, not evidence of simultaneous agreement everywhere.

claimLedger.evidence: Augustine advises weighing the reception of books among churches. His enumeration includes Tobit, Judith, two Maccabees, Wisdom and Sirach, as well as Esther and the 27 New Testament books.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: A different Old Testament scope coexists with the same New Testament enumeration seen in Athanasius.
claimLedger.limit: His account of authority is an argument within a church tradition, not a neutral survey. Ancient counts and book divisions differ.

claimLedger.evidence: In his prologue to Solomon’s books, Jerome separates Wisdom and Sirach from canonical Scripture while allowing edifying reading. He compares their use with Judith, Tobit and Maccabees.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: His concern is what can establish church doctrine. A translated or read work need not have that status in his account. Compare Augustine’s recognition of Wisdom and Sirach in the same broad period.
claimLedger.limit: This prologue states a position; it is not a survey of all Latin churches or a complete account of every use Jerome makes of these books.

claimLedger.evidence: The Peshitta New Testament has twenty-two books, without 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude and Revelation. The Gorgias reference entry dates its emergence as the standard version to around 400.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: A Greek or Latin list does not describe every contemporary Christian collection. Translation and transmission have their own histories.
claimLedger.limit: This describes the Peshitta version, not every later Syriac Bible or the present canon of every Syriac church. A version’s emergence and the date of an extant copy are separate questions.

claimLedger.evidence: Canon 24 of the African Code limits reading under the name of divine Scripture to an enumerated collection, including Tobit, Judith and two Maccabees. Its New Testament corresponds to 27 books.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: A church decision regulates received practice and seeks wider confirmation; it does not create the texts or their first use.
claimLedger.limit: The 419 compilation transmits earlier decisions, associated with Hippo (393) and Carthage (397). Those dates should not be treated as three independent surviving transcripts. Its jurisdiction is not the whole Christian world.

claimLedger.evidence: After Revelation, Alexandrinus preserves 1 Clement and part of 2 Clement. A contents list in volume 1 also names Psalms of Solomon, separated by a space; that work is not preserved in the codex.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: The surviving leaves and the contents list offer different evidence. The catalogue infers loss; the named work cannot be inspected here as surviving text.
claimLedger.limit: The arrangement establishes a collection, not equal canonical rank for every component. The damaged ending prevents a complete description from surviving leaves alone.

claimLedger.evidence: Bava Batra 14b transmits an order of the Prophets and Writings. The latter begins with Ruth, Psalms and Job, and ends with Ezra and Chronicles.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: Naming and ordering books is another way a collection is made visible. Order need not match that of a later printed Tanakh.
claimLedger.limit: The date of a compilation is not automatically the date of every tradition it preserves. This study does not date this list to a single year.

claimLedger.evidence: Trent’s fourth session receives a named set of Old and New Testament books with their parts, including Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and two Maccabees.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: The decree gives a binding Catholic definition amid Reformation controversy. Earlier lists already attest much of this collection.
claimLedger.limit: This decision does not describe the canon of every Jewish or Christian tradition. The decree’s Vulgate wording also concerns the received parts of books.

claimLedger.evidence: Chapter 1 enumerates 39 Old Testament and 27 New Testament books, then excludes the writings it calls Apocrypha from the canon.
claimLedger.reconstructionOrInterpretation: A shared New Testament collection does not erase disagreement about other writings or about how their authority is established.
claimLedger.limit: The linked OPC edition is a received denominational form, not a facsimile of the original assembly manuscript. It represents Reformed reception, not every Protestant practice.

claimLedger.claim: Two interpretations of a variable psalm collection require different assumptions about prior collections and use.
claimLedger.locator: Lim author manuscript pp. 18–23; LOC object description
claimLedger.limit: 11Q5 use cannot be established by order alone; no invented probabilities.

claimLedger.claim: The familiar “Council of Jamnia” narrative is a scholarly reconstruction, not the form of this source. Lim reviews its nineteenth-century formulation and later criticism. Rejecting that narrative does not supply a precise replacement date for closure.
claimLedger.limit: Does not settle the date when boundaries became fixed.

claimLedger.claim: Revelation appears conditionally in two categories in the same chapter.
claimLedger.limit: No quantitative inference about how many churches accepted it.

claimLedger.claim: Psalms of Solomon is named in the contents list but its text does not survive here.
claimLedger.status: Catalogue observation with custodial inference of loss
claimLedger.locator: Royal MS 1 D VIII contents 33; Royal MS 1 D V f. 4r
claimLedger.limit: Catalogue checked; images unavailable. No exact lost-leaf reconstruction.

expansionLimits: No direct inspection or collation of Alexandrinus images; catalogue explicitly reports images unavailable.
Gallagher–Meade, Mroczek, Hahneman and Guignard full works not accessed; their access limits appear on the page.
Sanders’s 1965 edition and early responses are bibliographically located, not claimed as read.
Syriac account concerns the historical Peshitta version, not a census of living churches.
Samaritan, Armenian, Georgian and other reception histories remain outside this selected study.
Comparison covers selected writings and named institutional descriptions, not exhaustive tradition-wide inventories.
